title: Preparing to go
tomorrow: Baba's in the hospital now. what do you do at a bedside?

cards: Somewhere in your contacts, maybe, is a name you scroll past on purpose. Baba Kartar has one. He asks Simran to find it, because the screen is too small for him: Gurnam.
They drove trucks together once, then fell out over money, and that was that, for a very long time. Simran dials and hands it over. It rings and rings.
A man's voice answers, older and rougher than she expected. Gurnam, Baba says. It's Kartar.
Then nobody says anything at all, and Simran isn't sure whether to leave the room.

teach.b: Earlier that week Baba had asked Harjit for a folder: his papers, his wishes, one page that says keep it simple. Plans are part of getting ready. But the Sikh picture of getting ready is bigger than a folder.
Kirtan Sohila, the prayer before sleep, opens on a wedding.
Guru Nanak writes, on Ang 12, in paraphrase: the day of the wedding is already written; come, friends, pour oil on the threshold, and give me your blessing to meet my Lord.

teach.h: FRIENDS POUR OIL AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: The soul is the bride, death is the day she goes to meet her groom, and her friends gather to get her ready.
Here's the thing to tell someone tonight: the Sikh bedtime prayer begins on a wedding day, and the wedding is the soul's going home. Getting ready means papers, and it also means people.
Kabir, whose verses are in the Granth, puts it plainly, on Ang 1372, in paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, God himself is there. On the phone, Gurnam finally speaks.
Kartar, you fool, he says. What took you so long? Both of them are laughing, and one of them is crying.

how: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and it is also sung at the end of a life; families facing an elder's last season make practical plans and try to settle old quarrels.

o: making plans and making peace before the end
packing a bag for a long trip abroad
moving an elder into a care home

s: in Kirtan Sohila, death is pictured as a wedding day
Ang 12: the day is written; friends gather to send the bride to her Lord.
preparing to go is mostly paperwork: a will and a plan
plans matter, and so does peace made with people while there's time.
Kabir's verse says God is where there is forgiveness
Ang 1372, in paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, God himself is there.

games.q: your mom and her sister haven't spoken since a fight over your grandfather's house. your grandmother is getting frail. what does today suggest?
o: stay out of it; it's their fight, not yours.
wait until after the funeral, when things calm down.
offer to help your mom write the first line to her sister now.
games.why: Kabir: where forgiveness is, God is. Baba Kartar didn't wait for a funeral; he made the call while there was time.

practice: Think of one person where something is unfinished between you: a small hurt, a silence that went on too long. While the sit runs, write the first line of a message to them.
Send it if it feels right, or save it as a version; one honest line is a start.

wordCard.voice: Preparing to go. In Kirtan Sohila the last day is a wedding day; getting ready means plans, and peace made while there's time.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: khima, forgiveness; in Kabir's verse, where there is khima, God is.

carryVoice: For the rest of today: make peace, one line at a time, before it's a folder. Done for now.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (Kirtan Sohila, Raag Gauri Deepaki, Guru Nanak: the wedding day written, oil on the threshold), paraphrased
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372 (Salok Kabir: 'jahaa khimaa tah aap'), paraphrased
